newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T. says tobacco deal ends uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T. says tobacco deal ends uncertainty.

text.p: B.A.T Industries Plc said on Friday that a landmark settlement between tobacco companies and U.S. states would cut its profits but would end the uncertainty that has been hanging over the industry.

"If you are looking at our company in the U.S. having to increase prices to fund its part of the settlement, that is going to reduce volumes and profits," B.A.T. spokesman Michael Prideaux told Reuters.
"But at least people should now be able to value the profits irrespective of the impending litigation," he said. "At least the agreement should get a bit of certainty into our lives."
B.A.T is the owner of Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., the third largest cigarette-maker in the United States. Its brands include Kent and Lucky Strike.
Under the agreement between U.S. states and the industry, tobacco companies will pay $368.5 billion over 25 years in compensation for the cost of treating smoking-related illnesses.
The companies were also required to concede that tobacco is addictive and agreed to accept extensive regulation over their products and advertising.
In exchange, the industry will be granted immunity from further liability for past deceptions or conspiracy.

London share analysts said earlier on Friday that B.A.T.'s shares were likely to rise to about six pounds when they resume trading on Monday because of the greater clarity any settlement would bring. The shares closed up 4-1/2 at 586-1/2 pence on Friday.
"Any settlement is viewed as good news (for the shares)," said Mark Duffy, tobacco industry analyst at SBC Warburg.
Prideaux said that all U.S. tobacco companies would have to raise prices to meet the cost of the settlement.
"They (cigarette prices) are going to rise quite steeply in the first year and in smaller stages in the years following," he said.
He said this would result in a drop in the number of cigarettes sold in the United States -- a figure which was already on the decline.
"In response to a significant price increase you are probably going to get fewer people smoking, or people who do smoke smoking less," said Prideaux.

Britain's largest cigarette maker Gallaher, which was hived off from American Brands and floated on the London stock market last month, said it would be unaffected by the settlement and would fight any similar attempt at litigation in Britain.

"We have complete confidence in the law and judicial process in the U.K. and we are not guided by the development in the U.S.," said a spokesman for Gallaher, whose brands include Benson and Hedges and Silk Cut.
